assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks (Lamb-Dicke trapping at the magic wavelength, Sr/Yb with fractional uncertainty near 1e-18) turned the atom into a quantitatively controlled probe: clocks now resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres and constrain variation of constants. It is precision atomic physics at its best, a clear, original and lasting advance in measuring time.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first demonstrated it; Ye's JILA group drove the accuracy and stability records and the many-body (Fermi-degenerate) clock. Two laureates is a clean, fair configuration. Others (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Kasevich-style networks) contributed, but the core credit is unusually clear.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent laboratories (Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, Paris, Wuhan) reproduce and extend the results; the interpretation is stable and the field is mature. Recognition is timely, and arguably overdue relative to the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with prior prizes (frequency combs, trapped-ion control) may make some members see it as incremental.
I cannot independently verify the exact current record uncertainties.
Whether a third credit (e.g. a theory/ion-clock figure) is warranted is not resolved by the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling a mechanical oscillator to its quantum ground state and controlling it with light or circuits addresses the question I find most compelling: where does the quantum world end and the classical one begin? Massive objects prepared in Fock states, squeezed states and entangled states is original, clear and conceptually deep, with applications to sensing that were not the motivation.
assessment.attribution: Cleland (with O'Connell/Martinis) gave the first ground state and single-phonon control in a piezo resonator; Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer drove sideband cooling and cavity optomechanics. The supplied names cover the central lines, but Teufel/Lehnert and Painter (not in the list) made equally decisive ground-state demonstrations, so the allocation is not clean.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in several platforms by independent groups and the interpretation is stable. The field is mature enough for recognition, though the most striking claims (massive-object entanglement, tests of collapse models) are still developing.
uncertainties: Credit is disputed between microwave, optical and piezoelectric platforms; omitted figures such as Teufel, Lehnert, Painter and Harris could be argued as decisive.
Some of the most interesting fundamental tests (gravity-related decoherence) remain inconclusive.
The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits may leave the committee wary of a closely related topic.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard models with tunable parameters: the superfluid-Mott transition, single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopes, and quantitative simulation of many-body physics. It is a conceptually new way to study strongly correlated matter, with lasting impact across AMO and condensed matter.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch, Cirac, Gardiner) proposed the optical-lattice Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner and Bloch (with Hansch) observed the Mott transition and developed the quantum gas microscope. Jaksch is not on the list and Cirac is, so a three-name set is a judgement; the experiment-theory split is natural but the experimental credit is spread over several groups (Esslinger, Greiner, Bloch, Gross, Kuhr).
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced and extended for over twenty years; stable. Some early quantum-simulation promises (e.g. unambiguous d-wave superconductivity in Fermi-Hubbard) are still unproven, but the established results are robust. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: The prize might overlap with the 2001 BEC prize and 2012 prize for quantum control in the minds of some members.
Exact attribution among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Zoller, Cirac and Jaksch is contestable.
Impact on strongly correlated condensed matter problems is still partly prospective.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and the Berry phase show that gauge potentials and geometry have physical consequences in quantum mechanics, a conceptually foundational insight with reach into molecular, optical and condensed-matter physics, including the quantum Hall effect and topological matter. This is discovery about how nature works, not technology.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) predicted the effect; Bohm died in 1992, so a prize could name Aharonov only on that strand, while Berry (1984) is clear for the geometric phase. Simon, Wilczek-Zee and Pancharatnam are also part of the story; the two-name set mixes two related but distinct discoveries.
assessment.maturity: Both effects were experimentally confirmed repeatedly (Chambers, Tonomura; optical and NMR Berry-phase experiments) over decades. Interpretation is stable, so the work is highly mature; the risk is that recognition is very late.
uncertainties: Compound candidate: Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phase may need separate treatment.
Posthumous issue for Bohm and credit overlap with Pancharatnam, Simon and others.
Whether the committee views this as an experimental-discovery-led prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brings strong light-matter coupling to engineered superconducting circuits, enabling dispersive readout, photon-number resolution and the foundation of superconducting quantum processors. It is a rich quantum-optics platform with real physical insight (strong coupling at the single-photon level in a solid-state device).
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and collaborators proposed the architecture; Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling in 2004. Four credited names exceed the three-laureate limit and Blais or Girvin must be traded off, which is not obviously fair; the original proposal is a theory-experiment collaboration.
assessment.maturity: Replicated across many laboratories and now an industry standard; the physics is stable. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes timing delicate, and the technology-driven side (quantum computing) is not the main criterion for me.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize and the 2012 prize on quantum control may make recognition seem premature or redundant.
Who is excluded among Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf, Wallraff is a real allocation difficulty.
The fundamental novelty vs. engineering contribution is debatable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry uses matter-wave coherence for precision measurements of gravity, rotation and fundamental constants. It extends the interferometric tradition to atoms and tests foundations of quantum mechanics and relativity; the original insight, coherent splitting of atoms with light and gratings, is clear and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard (first atom interferometer with gratings, 1991), Bordé (Ramsey-Bordé interferometer theory and early implementation), and Kasevich (Chu's group, then atom gravimeters and gyroscopes) are credible, but Chu, Keith, Mlynek, and Rasel's groups also made key demonstrations. The three-name set is defensible but not unambiguous.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups and used in commercial gravimeters; large-scale tests are ongoing. Mature but with continuing development, so timing is acceptable though some highlights (e.g. gravitational-wave detection by atoms) remain prospective.
uncertainties: Credit overlaps with the 1997 prize (laser cooling) and potentially Steven Chu.
Attribution between Bordé and the early experimental teams has historical disagreement.
Impact on fundamental tests is mostly precision rather than a decisive new discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators identified a new class of matter with protected edge or surface states, whose theory (Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang) and experiment (HgTe, then Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3) form a clear, original and influential chain. It adds a new principle to band theory.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele proposed the Z2 invariant; Molenkamp's group observed quantised edge transport in HgTe; Hasan (3D, ARPES) is also named, but B034 has four names and only three can be selected. Bernevig, Zhang, Fu and Moore, not in the list, were also decisive, so I regard the supplied credit as incomplete and the fair configuration as contested. I have not verified any claims about the nominal credit.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by independent groups and well understood; the field is mature. The 2016 prize on topological phase transitions partly overlaps but this is a distinct discovery. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Missing key names (Zhang, Bernevig, Fu, Moore) may undermine the proposed configuration.
Overlap with B006 and B036 (related topological candidates) means the committee would likely need to choose one framing.
I defer to condensed-matter colleagues on the relative merits.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade yields strongly interacting, individually addressable neutral atoms in programmable tweezer arrays, used for quantum simulation of spin models and for quantum gates. It combines careful atomic physics with a compelling new platform for many-body quantum matter.
assessment.attribution: Lukin (theory of blockade with Jaksch and Cirac, and large programmable arrays), Browaeys and Grangier (blockade experiments, 2009-2010), Saffman (gate proposals and demonstrations) are all substantial, but Jaksch, Gallagher, Pillet, Weiss, Regal and others also contributed. The four-name list exceeds three, and excluding Grangier is a hard choice.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by multiple groups, but the field is still moving quickly and the most striking results (large-scale error-corrected processors, quantum advantage claims) are recent. The ultimate lasting scientific impact is not yet settled, so recognition risks being premature.
uncertainties: Maturity is lower than for other AMO candidates on my list.
Attribution between blockade physics, tweezer arrays and quantum-computing demonstrations is entangled.
Some claims (quantum advantage, error correction) depend on rapidly evolving evidence I cannot verify.
